name: Auditing Smart Contracts
title: Auditing Smart Contracts
answer: Auditing smart contracts in digital asset accounting covers the code and controls that produce balances, transfers, fees, and obligations recorded on a blockchain. It also covers the accounting assertions that depend on that code, such as existence, completeness, valuation, rights and obligations, and presentation. The scope includes the contract logic, the permissions around it, and the offchain systems that feed it or read from it. It does not cover the legal ownership of a token or the fair value of a digital asset by itself, those are separate questions.

sections.body: Auditing smart contracts in digital asset accounting covers the code and controls that produce balances, transfers, fees, and obligations recorded on a blockchain. It also covers the accounting assertions that depend on that code, such as existence, completeness, valuation, rights and obligations, and presentation. The scope includes the contract logic, the permissions around it, and the offchain systems that feed it or read from it. It does not cover the legal ownership of a token or the fair value of a digital asset by itself, those are separate questions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on blockchain nodes and archive nodes that can replay state, on testnets that mirror mainnet behavior, and on block explorers and indexers that expose transactions and event logs. Auditors also use version control, reproducible build tools, and CI pipelines to compile source code and compare it with deployed bytecode. Static analyzers, fuzzers, symbolic execution engines, and formal verification tools run alongside manual review, and AI tools may help triage patterns or summarize findings. The infrastructure must preserve evidence, so logs, hashes, and build artifacts are stored in a way that can be checked later.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with scoping, gathering the contracts, the deployment records, and the accounting questions the code is meant to answer. Auditors read the source code, compare it to the deployed bytecode, and trace the paths that move value, mint tokens, change permissions, or call external contracts. They then test those paths with unit tests, fuzzing, symbolic execution, and formal proofs where the risk justifies it, and they simulate economic scenarios such as oracle failure, liquidation, or a run on withdrawals. Findings are written up with severity, evidence, and a reproduction path, then the team fixes the code and the auditor retests the fix. The final report states what was reviewed, what was found, what was fixed, and what remains open.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in smart contract auditing turn on who owns the code, who has the right to review it, and who is allowed to change it. Audit reports are often confidential, but they may be shared with investors, regulators, or counterparties, and engagement letters typically define scope, liability, and permitted use. Provenance matters because the deployed bytecode must match the audited source, and the compiler, dependencies, and build settings must be recorded. For digital asset accounting, the audit trail supports internal controls, segregation of duties, change management, and the evidence behind financial statement assertions. This is a description of practice, not legal advice, and it does not tell a reader how to treat a particular token or transaction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Smart contract auditing is moving toward continuous monitoring, where onchain alerts and automated checks run after deployment rather than only before it. AI assisted review is likely to handle more pattern detection, code summarization, and anomaly triage, while human auditors keep responsibility for judgment and sign off. Formal verification and reproducible builds are becoming more common for high value contracts, and accounting teams are asking for audit evidence that maps directly to ledger entries and disclosures. The limits remain, because code can be correct and the economic design can still fail, and because offchain data, governance, and key management sit outside the contract. The direction is better tooling, clearer standards, and tighter links between code audit, financial audit, and compliance review.
